conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and a lot of ostomy output. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain started a few days ago—sharp and crampy, mostly on the right side. And my ostomy bag has been filling up so fast, I’m changing it 8 to 10 times a day. It’s green and watery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea, yes, but no vomiting. I haven’t been eating much—just sipping fluids. And I had a fever at home, about 102, but Tylenol and Dilaudid helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from the ER. It shows thickening in part of your small intestine near the surgical connection. That could explain the pain and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection? Or could it be the lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Right now, we’re thinking it’s likely enteritis—probably viral. We’ve ruled out C. diff and other bacterial infections. Your lymphoma is still in remission based on your last PET scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. But why so much fluid loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflamed bowel isn’t absorbing fluids properly. That’s why you’re losing so much. We’ve started IV fluids and will keep monitoring your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling weak. Is that from the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your labs show low potassium, which can make you feel tired and weak. We’re giving you potassium through the IV and will send more blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about my transplant? Is this GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that. But GVHD usually causes bloody diarrhea and weight loss over time. Your symptoms came on quickly, and your stool tests are negative for blood and infection markers. It’s less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your essential ones—methadone for pain, tacrolimus for transplant, and your asthma and thyroid meds. We held metformin since you’re not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics I got in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing cipro and flagyl for now, just in case there’s a bacterial cause. But if all tests stay negative, we’ll stop them and let your body clear the virus on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and CMV test came back negative. No sign of those infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the stool tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also negative—for C. diff, salmonella, parasites, everything. The viral culture is still pending, but it’s looking more like viral enteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just need to ride it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pretty much. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and electrolytes. Your fever’s gone down, and your pain is better with Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the fever’s gone. I was worried it meant something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign. We’ll keep watching your labs. Your platelets and white count are low, but they’ve been that way since your transplant, so we’re not too concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ostomy output has decreased—from over a liter a day to about 500 mL. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I only changed my bag three times last night. That’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to stop the IV antibiotics today since all tests are negative. You’ll go home on a short course of oral cipro and metronidazole just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit low. We’ll send you home with potassium pills for three days. Make sure to take them with food to avoid stomach upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more blood transfusions? My hemoglobin was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 8.0 now, which is low but stable. Since you’re not bleeding and feeling okay, we won’t transfuse. It should improve as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tacrolimus level? I remember last time it was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it this morning. It’s <2.0, which is low. But since you’re on sirolimus now too, we’ll let your transplant team adjust it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool viral culture came back negative—no virus found. That supports our diagnosis of self-limited enteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was probably just a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Your body fought it off. You’re eating again, your output is near normal, and you’re not febrile. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop fever, severe pain, or if your ostomy output increases again. Keep taking the antibiotics and potassium as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with your transplant team and oncologist. They’ll monitor your counts and overall status. Also, keep taking your budesonide—it helps with bowel inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge. Your vitals are stable, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discharge you around noon. You’ll take home prescriptions for the antibiotics, potassium, and your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin? I see it on the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a precaution. It’s oral vancomycin, which stays in the gut. It’s to prevent any C. diff, especially since you’ve been on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And sirolimus—why was that added?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your transplant team started it to help with immune regulation. It works with tacrolimus. Take it at 6 a.m. as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that. Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep up with your IVIG every four weeks. It’s important for your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have it scheduled. I won’t miss it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be in touch. Bye.
